newsitem.title: USA: Democrats post gains in U.S. House races.
newsitem.headline: Democrats post gains in U.S. House races.

text.p: With five U.S. House of Representatives races still undecided on Thursday, Democrats appeared to have gained at least nine seats from the majority Republicans in Tuesday's voting, according to both parties.
But Republicans increased their Senate majority to 54-45 from the current 53-47, with one race in Oregon undecided.

California Republican Representative Bob Dornan is leading Democrat Loretta Sanchez by 223 votes with a few thousand absentee ballots to count, and Pennsylvania Republican Representative Jon Fox is 10 votes ahead of Democrat Joe Hoeffel, with a recount set.
Three races for redrawn districts in Texas will be settled by Dec. 10 runoffs after open primaries on Tuesday. One matches two Republicans to replace retiring Republican Jack Fields.
In the other two, Republican incumbent Steve Stockman faces Democrat Nick Lampson and Democrat Representative Ken Bentsen meets Republican Dolly McKenna.

If Dornan, Fox, Stockman and Bentsen all win, the House party lineup when the next session of Congress begins on Jan. 7 will be 227 Republicans, 207 Democrats and one independent, Bernard Sanders of Vermont.
The House had 235 Republicans, 197 Democrats and one independent when it recessed in October. There were two vacancies, one in each party.

Democrats defeated 18 Republican incumbents on Tuesday, including 13 of the 70 Republican freshmen running for re-election, and won four seats held by retiring Republicans. But Republicans beat three Democratic incumbents and won 10 seats of retiring Democrats.

In Oregon, Republican Gordon Smith leads Democrat Tom Bruggere by about 16,000 votes in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Mark Hatfield, but half a million mail ballots remain to be counted.
If Smith wins, Republicans will have gained two Senate seats. A Bruggere victory will cut the net gain to one.
Republicans picked up seats of retiring Democrats in Alabama, Arkansas and Nebraska while Democrat Representative Tim Johnson defeated Republican Sen. Larry Pressler in South Dakota.

There will be nine women in the Senate next year with the victories of Republican Susan Collins in Maine and Democrat Mary Landrieu in Louisiana offsetting the retirements of Kansas Republicans Nancy Kassebaum and Sheila Frahm.
Frahm replaced Bob Dole when he quit in June, but lost a primary election to Representative Sam Brownback, who won on Tuesday.
Illinois Democrat Carol Moseley-Braun remains as the only black senator.
There will be at least 50 women in the House next year, one more than this session, and 39 blacks, a decline of one.
